strengths: Presents a unified, versatile framework (OmniX) that repurposes pre-trained 2D flow matching priors for a broad set of panoramic tasks—perception (RGB→X: depth, normal, albedo, roughness, metallic), generation (image-to-panorama), and completion (mask-guided inpainting)—under a single formulation with modular cross-modal LoRA adapters, which is an elegant and practically useful design.

Introduces PanoX, a new synthetic panoramic dataset with dense geometry and PBR material annotations spanning both indoor and outdoor scenes rendered in Unreal Engine 5, filling a genuine gap since prior panoramic datasets largely lack PBR/material annotations or outdoor coverage; the dataset and its train/val/test/out-domain splits could be a useful community resource.

Demonstrates a clear application pipeline from single image to graphics-ready 3D scene (mesh + textures + PBR maps) enabling relighting, PBR rendering, and physics simulation in Blender, going beyond typical 2D-lifting works that only handle appearance/geometry.

Provides reasonably thorough quantitative comparisons against multiple strong, recent baselines (RGB↔X, MGNet, IDArb, IID, DiffusionRenderer, DepthAnyCamera, DepthAnywhere, OmniData-v2, MoGe) on out-of-domain test data, showing consistent improvements on intrinsic decomposition and competitive geometry estimation.

Includes informative ablations comparing adapter architectures (Shared-Branch vs Shared-Adapter vs Separate-Adapter) and analyzing the effect of camera-ray conditioning, joint vs independent material/geometry modeling, which help justify design choices.

The paper is transparent about limitations (distance estimation still imprecise leading to bumpy geometry, poor metallic generalization, inherited inefficiency of diffusion-based backbones), which strengthens the credibility of the claims.
weaknesses: The PanoX dataset is quite small in scene diversity: only 8 total 3D scenes (5 indoor, 3 outdoor), split into train/val/test and a 2-scene out-domain set; generalization claims based on such limited underlying scene diversity are somewhat weak despite the ~10,000 instances/60,000 images figure, since these are all renders from very few base scenes/environments.

Evaluation for intrinsic decomposition and geometry estimation is conducted primarily on PanoX-OutDomain, which is synthetic and generated by the authors themselves; there is limited quantitative evaluation on independent real-world or established panoramic benchmarks (e.g., Structured3D test split is used for training but not clearly used for held-out quantitative comparison), raising concerns about evaluation independence and potential dataset bias favoring the proposed method's synthetic domain.

No quantitative evaluation is provided for the panoramic generation (image-to-panorama) and completion (inpainting) components—only qualitative figures are shown; typical metrics such as FID, CLIP-score, or user studies for generation quality/diversity and completion fidelity are absent, making it hard to assess how these tasks compare against existing panorama generation/outpainting baselines (e.g., MVDiffusion, Text2Light, LayerPano3D).

The 3D scene construction quality (mesh reconstruction from distance maps, PBR-ready assets, physical simulation) is demonstrated only qualitatively via a few figures/videos; no quantitative metrics (e.g., geometric fidelity, rendering error, user study on realism) are reported for the downstream graphics-ready 3D scenes, which is the paper's central selling point.

The comparison methods for geometry estimation are a mix of panoramic and narrow-FoV models with differing training data scale (e.g., MoGe trained on 21 datasets) — while the paper acknowledges this, it complicates a fully fair comparison and the paper does not control for data scale in ablations.

Some technical details are thin: e.g., how camera intrinsics/masking for occlusion-aware sampling interact with the flow matching objective, how multiple LoRAs are combined at inference for the full 3-stage pipeline, and computational cost/runtime of the full pipeline (12 adapters, iterative ODE solving) are not clearly reported, affecting reproducibility.

The paper's own limitations note that Euclidean distance prediction leads to 'bumpy' 3D surfaces and that metallic prediction generalizes poorly, both of which directly undermine the core claim of producing 'graphics-ready' assets for PBR rendering and simulation; these issues are significant given the paper's central contribution claim.

The related work and framing position this primarily as an Algorithms/General contribution, but a substantial portion of the contribution (PanoX) is a Dataset/Benchmark contribution; the dataset description lacks some details expected for benchmark contributions (e.g., licensing, exact scene names/sources, diversity statistics beyond scene count, dataset release/maintenance plan).

strengths: Addresses a clear and practical gap in panorama-based 2D lifting for 3D scene generation: most prior work generates appearance only and relies on off-the-shelf depth estimators, ignoring intrinsic PBR properties needed for graphics pipelines. OmniX unifies generation, perception (RGB→X for depth/normal/albedo/roughness/metallic), and completion within a single adapter-based framework built on a pretrained flow matching model (FLUX.1-dev).

The proposed Separate-Adapter cross-modal architecture is a sensible and well-motivated design choice, and the paper provides a clean ablation (Table 4) comparing it against Shared-Branch and Shared-Adapter alternatives, showing consistent and fairly large improvements.

The PanoX dataset fills a genuine gap: to the authors' knowledge it is the first panoramic dataset with both indoor and outdoor scenes and dense geometry + material (PBR) annotations, which could be a useful community resource independent of the specific model.

Extensive quantitative comparisons against multiple strong recent baselines (RGB↔X, MGNet, IDArb, IID, DiffusionRenderer, MoGe, DepthAnyCamera, DepthAnywhere, OmniData-v2) across intrinsic decomposition and geometry estimation tasks, with OmniX achieving state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art results, especially decisive margins on albedo/roughness/metallic.

The end-to-end pipeline from single image to graphics-ready 3D scene (mesh + PBR textures) with demonstrated downstream applications (free exploration, PBR relighting, physical simulation in Blender) is a compelling and practically useful demonstration of the framework's utility beyond pure benchmark numbers.

The paper includes a good faith limitations discussion (bumpy geometry from imperfect distance prediction, poor metallic generalization, inherited slow inference from diffusion backbone) which strengthens credibility rather than overselling results.
Additional ablations in the appendix (joint vs. independent material/geometry modeling, camera ray inputs) show a thoughtful design exploration rather than just reporting a single best configuration.
weaknesses: The PanoX dataset covers only 8 total scenes (5 indoor, 3 outdoor), which is quite small in scene diversity despite yielding 60,000 rendered images (likely via many viewpoints/augmentations within few environments). This raises concern about how well the reported PanoX-OutDomain generalization evaluation (drawn from only 2 held-out scenes) reflects true out-of-domain robustness, and about the diversity/representativeness of the 'large-scale' claim.

The comparison in Tables 2-3 uses PanoX-OutDomain as the evaluation set, which is synthetic Unreal Engine data most similar in style to OmniX's own training distribution (PanoX-Train); competitor baselines were trained on different data distributions, so the comparison may somewhat favor OmniX rather than reflecting genuinely fair cross-domain generalization comparisons. In-the-wild qualitative results are shown but not quantitatively evaluated.

No evaluation of the panoramic generation (image-to-panorama) or completion (inpainting) quality against quantitative metrics (e.g., FID, CLIP-based consistency) or baselines such as MVDiffusion, LayerPano3D, or other panorama outpainting methods -- only qualitative appendix figures are provided for these components, despite them being core claimed contributions.

The 3D scene construction pipeline (mesh reconstruction from distance map + UV texture assignment) is only qualitatively demonstrated (Figure 8) without any quantitative evaluation of mesh quality, PBR rendering fidelity, or comparison against alternative scene reconstruction/lifting baselines (e.g., LayerPano3D, DreamCube), making it hard to assess how much this final pipeline stage improves over related concurrent work.

The metallic prediction (a key PBR channel) is explicitly noted by the authors to generalize poorly, and normal/distance joint modeling ablation shows no benefit -- these findings, while honestly reported, indicate the geometry/material perception backbone is not yet robust enough for reliably 'graphics-ready' output, undercutting the central claim in the title.

Camera ray input ablation (Table 5) shows negligible or even negative effects on most modalities, raising a question about why this component is included as part of the described method versus being an unnecessary/marginal addition.

Reproducibility could be improved: architectural and training details for the 12 separately trained adapter models are relatively sparse (e.g., mask sampling hyperparameters, exact LoRA ranks, adapter architecture specifics for each task variant), and code/dataset release status is not explicitly confirmed in the main text.

strengths: Presents a genuinely unified framework covering panorama generation, multimodal (geometry+PBR material) perception, and mask-guided completion within a single formulation, repurposing a pretrained 2D flow-matching backbone via lightweight modality-specific LoRA adapters.

Circular Synchronization is a clean, well-motivated, training-free solution to seam discontinuities that operates at the level of spatial operators (attention/convolution) rather than post-hoc latent blending, and is shown qualitatively to outperform circular blending and latent rotation baselines.

Introduces PanoX, a new synthetic panorama dataset with dense pixel-aligned geometry and PBR material annotations spanning both indoor and outdoor scenes, filling a genuine gap relative to existing datasets that lack either panoramic coverage, material labels, or outdoor scenes (Table 1 comparison is informative).

Extensive empirical validation across three sub-tasks (generation, intrinsic decomposition, geometry estimation) against numerous strong and recent baselines (CubeDiff, DiffusionRenderer, MoGe, IDArb, etc.), with consistent state-of-the-art or competitive results and reasonably thorough ablations (adapter architecture, prior transfer, camera-ray conditioning, PBR channel packing, joint vs. independent modality modeling).

Demonstrates an end-to-end, practically useful application: converting predicted panoramic modalities into a graphics-ready 3D mesh usable for relighting, free exploration, and physical simulation in a standard engine (Blender), which supports the paper's stated goal of producing PBR-ready assets rather than merely appearance-only reconstructions.
weaknesses: PanoX is built from only eight Unreal Engine environments (5 indoor, 3 outdoor); despite the large image count, the diversity of underlying 3D scenes is small, raising concerns about how much of the reported generalization (e.g., PanoX-OutDomain, in-the-wild results) reflects true robustness versus dataset/style overfitting; in-the-wild perception results are only shown qualitatively with no quantitative evaluation.

The paper's central claim of enabling 'graphics-ready' PBR scenes is somewhat undercut by its own admitted limitations: distance/geometry predictions are described as producing 'bumpy' surfaces that affect PBR rendering quality, and metallic prediction generalizes poorly, which are core components of the claimed PBR pipeline.

Panorama generation results are mixed rather than uniformly dominant: on SUN360, OmniX has notably worse FID (39.4) than CubeDiff (25.5) despite better KID/CLIP-FID, so the 'state-of-the-art across both datasets' framing overstates the consistency of the improvement.

The scene-reconstruction stage (projecting distance maps to mesh, spherical UV unwrapping) is described only briefly with no quantitative evaluation of mesh quality, pole/seam artifacts in equirectangular-to-mesh conversion, or the fidelity of the final textured 3D asset beyond qualitative renders.

No quantitative or user-study evaluation of the final rendered/relit 3D scenes' perceptual quality or physical plausibility is provided; the application section relies solely on qualitative figures and supplementary videos.

Individual technical components (LoRA-based adapters, circular padding for equivariant panorama generation, flow-matching repurposing) are each incremental extensions of known techniques; the core novelty lies mainly in their unified combination and application to multimodal PBR panorama perception, which somewhat limits the conceptual originality despite strong engineering execution.
